It's October and it's already cold in Berlin. Mara only has a thin jacket from Sibiu. Lena goes shopping with her, to a shop on Schönhauser Allee.
Mara, this jacket is too thin for Berlin. In January it's minus ten degrees here!
It's cold in Sibiu too. But you're right, I need a coat.
Yes, please. I'm looking for a warm winter coat.

I like this red one here. Can I try it on?
Of course. The fitting room is back there.
Lena, what do you think? It's a bit too big, isn't it?
Yes, it doesn't fit you well. But the colour looks great on you!

One moment… Yes, here it is. In red and in black.
Perfect! It fits! And how much is it?

In foreign words, “v” is read “v”: Pullover, Video, Vase.
Some common verbs take the dative: helfen (to help), danken (to thank), gefallen, passen, stehen (to suit), gehören (to belong to), schmecken (to taste good).
“Gefallen” works like “to please” in English: the thing that is liked is the SUBJECT, and the person is in the dative (literally “the jacket pleases me”).
“gefallen” is for something you see; for food you use “schmecken” (Der Kuchen schmeckt mir), and for activities “gern” (Ich tanze gern).
“welcher” (which?) and “dieser” (this) are declined like the definite article: their endings look like der / die / das.
Which coat do you like? — This one.
Which colour do you want? — This one.

Mauerpark is only ten minutes from Kastanienallee. The Berlin Wall used to stand here. Today there's a huge flea market here every Sunday.
There's everything: old vinyl records, lamps from the sixties, bikes, books, crockery from the GDR and, of course, lots of clothes.
Lena and Mara arrive at eleven o'clock. Ludwig comes too. He says he just wants to stroll around, but Lena knows: Grandpa has been looking for an old tram lamp for years.
Fritz stays at home. At the flea market there are too many sausages and too many dogs.

First they walk slowly from one stall to the next. Lena buys an old tin cake mould. Mara tries on a hat with earflaps, but Lena laughs so loudly that Mara puts it back straight away. Ludwig looks very carefully at every stall with metal objects and says every time: “No, that's not it.”
At the third stall, Mara finds a coat. It's dark green, made of thick wool, with big wooden buttons. It isn't new, but it's wonderful.
Lena, look! This coat! What do you think?
There's no fitting room, just an old mirror hanging in a tree. Mara puts the coat on. It fits her perfectly, as if it had been made for her.
It suits you very well! It's genuine loden from Austria. Eighty euros.
Mara remembers Lena's advice: at the flea market you have to haggle.
Eighty? Hmm. It's nice, but there's a button missing here. Could you make it a bit cheaper? Fifty?
Sixty and I'll take it right now.
The seller looks at Mara, then at Lena, then at the coat. Then he laughs: “All right then. Sixty. Because it suits you so well.”
Suddenly they hear a shout. It's Ludwig! He's standing in front of a stall with old metal objects, holding something in his hands: a round yellow lamp.
This is it! A lamp from a Tatra tram! We had exactly these lamps in the seventies. Maybe it's even from my tram!
The lamp costs forty euros. Ludwig doesn't haggle. He pays straight away and carries it home like a baby.

In the evening, the yellow lamp hangs in the living room. Ludwig sits on his sofa and looks at it. Mara sits next to him, in her green coat, even though it's warm in the flat. She simply doesn't want to take it off.
Lena takes a photo of the two of them and sends it to Thomas in Munich. Ludwig asks: “How do you like the photo?” Thomas replies straight away: “Dad, you both look very happy.”
